summary: This note describes leadership and procedural roles in the United States Senate and the Senate's role in impeachment. It explains that the Vice President presides as President of the Senate, with the President Pro Tempore presiding in the Vice President's absence, and that floor leaders are elected by party majority and minority caucuses though not constitutional officers. It also summarizes impeachment outcomes: sixteen officials impeached, seven convicted, and two presidents impeached, both acquitted.
one_line: Overview of the U.S. Senate's presiding officers, party floor leaders, and its role in impeachment trials, including the two presidential impeachments.
key_facts: The Vice President of the United States is the presiding officer of the Senate and serves as President of the Senate.
In the Vice President's absence, the President Pro Tempore presides over the Senate.
The President Pro Tempore is customarily the senior member of the party holding a majority of seats.
In the early 20th century, majority and minority parties in the Senate began electing their floor leaders.
Floor leaders in the Senate are not constitutional officers.
The House of Representatives has impeached sixteen officials.
Seven of the sixteen officials impeached by the House have been convicted.
One impeached official resigned before the Senate could complete the trial.
Only two presidents of the United States have ever been impeached.
Both presidential impeachment trials ended in acquittal.
In Johnson's trial, the Senate fell one vote short of the two-thirds majority required for conviction.
